title: Paragraphs, coherence and transitions
note: A paragraph develops one main idea, usually announced in a topic sentence near the start. It has unity when every sentence serves that idea, and coherence when the sentences connect through repeated key terms, pronouns, parallel structure and transitions such as however, therefore and for example.

read.title: Building a paragraph
text: A paragraph is a unit of thought, not a unit of length. It should make one point and make it fully. Consider this example: "City trees do more than decorate streets. They cool the air by shading pavement and releasing water vapor. They also absorb rainwater that would otherwise flood storm drains. For these reasons, planting trees is one of the cheapest ways a city can prepare for hotter summers."

The first sentence is the topic sentence; it announces the claim. Each following sentence supports that claim, so the paragraph has unity. The sentences also connect. The pronoun they points back to trees, the word also signals an added point, and "For these reasons" gathers the evidence into a conclusion. These links give the paragraph coherence.

A paragraph loses unity when it drifts. If a sentence about the history of a city's parks appeared in the middle of the example, it would be interesting but off topic, and it would belong in a different paragraph. When you revise, read each paragraph's first sentence, then check every other sentence against it.

q.q: In the example, what does the topic sentence claim?
o: City trees do more than decorate streets

q.q: Which feature of the example builds coherence?
o: Its sentences are all the same length
It mentions the history of parks
The pronoun they points back to trees

q.q: Why would a sentence on park history hurt the example?
o: It would make the paragraph too long
It would break the paragraph's unity
